cur-b1-setup-tab-autocomplete.q: While renaming a variable, Tab highlights a suggestion at a different location in the file that you weren't expecting. What should you do?
options: Always press Tab automatically - predicted edits are always correct
Read the full suggestion before accepting - it may extend the rename to a similarly-named but unrelated variable
Immediately press Esc without reading, since any jump means the suggestion is wrong
Close and restart Cursor to reset the suggestion
cur-b1-setup-tab-autocomplete.why: Tab predicts your next several edits and can jump to another location in the file; a plausible-looking prediction isn't automatically correct, so reading it before accepting matters.

cur-b1-setup-tab-autocomplete.q: Why does the lesson recommend practicing Tab on a project you already know well, rather than an unfamiliar one?
options: Tab technically doesn't function on unfamiliar codebases
Tab only builds its predictions from projects you've indexed previously
You need to be able to judge whether a suggestion is actually correct, which you can't do on code you don't understand
It's simply faster to demo on a project you already know
cur-b1-setup-tab-autocomplete.why: Practicing on a project you already know lets you judge suggestion quality directly instead of trusting output you can't yet evaluate.

cur-b1-setup-tab-autocomplete.q: What is Tab explicitly NOT designed to do, per the lesson?
options: Predict follow-on edits after you make one manual change
Understand your intent from a plain-language description alone, with no edit yet started
Let you jump between several predicted edit sites
Operate across an entire file rather than just the current line
cur-b1-setup-tab-autocomplete.why: Expecting Tab to understand intent from nothing is a listed common mistake - it predicts from an edit pattern you start, not from a description of what you want.

cur-b2-chat-with-codebase.q: Why should you wait for codebase indexing to finish before asking Chat detailed architecture questions?
options: Indexing is purely cosmetic and has no effect on answer quality
Chat searches semantically across the whole project once indexed; asking too early produces a thinner or stale answer
Cursor technically blocks the Chat panel entirely until indexing completes
Indexing only affects Tab's suggestions, not Chat's answers
cur-b2-chat-with-codebase.why: Asking broad questions before indexing has finished is a listed common mistake, since Chat's semantic search depends on the index being complete.

cur-b2-chat-with-codebase.q: What does explicitly @-mentioning a specific folder in a Chat question accomplish?
options: It's purely cosmetic formatting with no functional effect
It disables Chat's semantic search for that question
It grounds the answer in exactly those files rather than a more generic, plausible-sounding explanation
It automatically switches Chat into an edit mode
cur-b2-chat-with-codebase.why: @-mentioning files or folders grounds the answer in Cursor's semantic index of your actual code, rather than a generic explanation the codebase might not actually support.

cur-b2-chat-with-codebase.q: Chat gives you a codebase tour with several cited file paths. What should you do before trusting it fully?
options: Immediately ask Chat to start making edits based on the tour in the same thread
Nothing further is needed, since Chat already cited real paths
Discard the tour entirely and redo the exploration using Agent mode instead
Open at least two of the cited files yourself to verify the explanation is accurate
cur-b2-chat-with-codebase.why: Trusting the explanation without opening any cited file is a listed common mistake; spot-checking two files confirms the tour matches the real code before you rely on it.

cur-i1-inline-edit-multi-file.q: You need to rename a shared TypeScript type used across 11 files. Which tool best fits this task?
options: Inline edit (Cmd+K), run separately 11 times
A multi-file edit describing the full rename across the project, reviewed file by file
Tab, since it automatically predicts follow-on edits everywhere in the project
None of Cursor's tools - this kind of rename must be done manually
cur-i1-inline-edit-multi-file.why: Multi-file edits coordinate a change across many files at once; doing 11 separate inline-edit reviews would waste time that a single coordinated, per-file-reviewed diff handles directly.

cur-i1-inline-edit-multi-file.q: A multi-file edit correctly updates 10 files but incorrectly also renamed an unrelated local variable in the 11th. What's the recommended response?
options: Reject the entire batch and restart the whole task from scratch
Accept all 11 files since the large majority are correct
Accept the 10 correct files and reject just the one wrong file, then send a targeted correction for it
Manually redo all 11 files by hand to be safe
cur-i1-inline-edit-multi-file.why: You can accept or reject changes per file rather than as one unit - rejecting only the wrong file and sending a targeted correction avoids throwing out a mostly-correct change.

cur-i1-inline-edit-multi-file.q: Why is inline edit (Cmd+K) the better choice for adding one optional parameter to a single function signature, rather than a multi-file edit?
options: Inline edit is scoped to the selection or current file, producing a tightly scoped diff you can read at a glance
Multi-file edit is technically incapable of touching function signatures
Inline edit must always run before any multi-file edit is allowed to start
There is no real functional difference between the two tools
cur-i1-inline-edit-multi-file.why: Using multi-file edits for a one-line, local fix is a listed common mistake - inline edit handles it faster with a smaller, easier-to-review diff.

cur-i2-agent-mode-whole-tasks.q: Ten minutes into an Agent-mode task, you notice it's clearly heading in the wrong direction. What should you do?
options: Wait until it reports done, then review the entire diff at once
Interrupt it early - redirecting mid-task is cheaper than reviewing a finished wrong diff
Let it keep going, since interrupting an Agent session isn't actually supported
Close Cursor entirely and start a brand-new session
cur-i2-agent-mode-whole-tasks.why: Letting Agent run unsupervised through an ambiguous or wrong-direction task instead of interrupting early is a listed common mistake.

cur-i2-agent-mode-whole-tasks.q: Why does the newsletter-validation task spec instruct Agent to check for an existing validation pattern before writing new logic?
options: It's required syntax that all Agent-mode prompts must include
Doing so intentionally slows the task down to improve the result
It prevents duplicate, inconsistent validation logic when a reusable pattern already exists in the codebase
It has no real effect on the resulting diff
cur-i2-agent-mode-whole-tasks.why: Checking for and reusing an existing utility, rather than writing new logic from scratch, avoids duplicated and inconsistent approaches to the same problem.

cur-i2-agent-mode-whole-tasks.q: When does the lesson say it's worth deliberately choosing a flagship model over Auto in Agent mode?
options: For architecture-sensitive or ambiguous work, since flagship models handle harder judgment calls at a higher usage-credit cost
Always, for every single task regardless of complexity
Never - Auto is described as sufficient for all cases
Only for one-line formatting fixes
cur-i2-agent-mode-whole-tasks.why: The lesson frames model choice as a cost lever: Auto suits routine, well-scoped tasks, while a flagship model is reserved for architecture-sensitive or ambiguous work.

cur-i3-rules-files-conventions.q: Your team keeps getting default-exported components and swallowed errors from Agent-generated code, despite repeating the convention in prompts. What's the better fix?
options: Keep repeating the convention manually in every future prompt
Write it once as a .cursor/rules/*.mdc file with alwaysApply: true, so it's applied to every future task automatically
Switch away from Cursor to a different AI coding tool
Disable Agent mode and rely only on Tab going forward
cur-i3-rules-files-conventions.why: Rules files exist precisely so a team encodes a convention once instead of re-explaining it in every prompt - alwaysApply makes it ambient across every task.

cur-i3-rules-files-conventions.q: What happens to a legacy root .cursorrules file when Agent mode runs?
options: It continues to work exactly as it always did
Agent mode ignores it entirely - it must be migrated into .cursor/rules/*.mdc files
Cursor automatically converts it to the new format on first use
It applies only to Tab suggestions, not to Agent tasks
cur-i3-rules-files-conventions.why: The lesson explicitly warns that legacy root .cursorrules files no longer work with Agent mode, and that leaving one in place unmigrated is a common mistake.

cur-i3-rules-files-conventions.q: Why does the lesson recommend citing a real file, like src/lib/logging.ts, inside a rule instead of describing the pattern abstractly?
options: File citations are a required part of the .mdc syntax
It gives Agent something concrete to imitate rather than an adjective to interpret
It reduces the overall size of the rule file
It's purely for documentation and has no effect on generated output
cur-i3-rules-files-conventions.why: Writing rules as vague aspirations instead of concrete, checkable conventions with a real file reference is a listed common mistake - a cited real file gives the Agent something specific to imitate.

cur-i4-debugging-workflows.q: Agent proposes a fix that makes a failing test pass by loosening its assertion. How should this be judged?
options: This is an acceptable minimal fix, since the test technically passes now
This is the exact risky shortcut the lesson warns against - it redefines correctness rather than fixing the underlying code
It's fine as long as no one notices the change
This is the lesson's recommended approach for stubborn bugs
cur-i4-debugging-workflows.why: An agent under pressure to make an error go away can take the fastest route, like loosening an assertion - the lesson explicitly frames this as patching the symptom instead of the cause.

cur-i4-debugging-workflows.q: Before proposing any fix, what must Agent do first per the lesson's process?
options: Immediately implement whichever fix looks most obvious
Actually reproduce the failure by running the command in the terminal and confirm it sees the same error
Skip reproduction whenever the stack trace looks familiar
Ask a teammate to reproduce the issue instead
cur-i4-debugging-workflows.why: Requiring Agent to reproduce the failure itself, not just read the pasted trace, rules out a fix based on a misread of the error.

cur-i4-debugging-workflows.q: If BugBot (automated review) flags a comment on your fix, what's the recommended response?
options: Treat it as mandatory and apply it without question
Treat it as a second check, not the final word - triage explicitly as fix or reject-with-reason, the same discipline as a human reviewer's comment
Ignore every BugBot comment by default as noise
Disable BugBot on the repository after the very first false positive
cur-i4-debugging-workflows.why: The proTip explicitly instructs treating automated review comments the same way you'd treat a human reviewer's - with deliberate, explicit triage, not blanket acceptance or dismissal.

cur-a1-background-cloud-agents.q: You want to dispatch three tasks as background/cloud agents to run in parallel. What must be true of them?
options: They should all touch the same core file for consistency
They must be independent and not touch the same files, since overlapping edits create conflicts you'll have to resolve manually
They should be as ambiguous as possible so the agent can use its own judgment
They must all be configured to use the exact same model
cur-a1-background-cloud-agents.why: Background and cloud agents run unsupervised and in parallel - dispatching tasks that touch overlapping files creates merge conflicts between two supposedly 'independent' agents.

cur-a1-background-cloud-agents.q: A cloud agent reports its task completed and that tests passed. What should you do before merging the result?
options: Trust the report and merge directly from the cloud environment
Pull the result down locally and run your own build/test suite before merging
Merge immediately, since cloud agents are described as always accurate
Re-dispatch the identical task again just to double-check
cur-a1-background-cloud-agents.why: Trusting a cloud agent's own claim that tests passed without rerunning them yourself locally is a listed common mistake.

cur-a1-background-cloud-agents.q: Which kind of task should be reserved for a live, supervised Agent session instead of background/cloud dispatch?
options: Adding unit tests to an already well-understood utility function
Genuinely ambiguous or high-stakes work, since no one is present to clarify mid-run
A minor, isolated dependency version bump
Adding JSDoc comments to existing exported functions
cur-a1-background-cloud-agents.why: The lesson explicitly reserves genuinely ambiguous or high-stakes work for a live, interruptible session rather than unsupervised background/cloud dispatch.

cur-a2-feature-delivery-workflow.q: Before starting implementation on a new ticket, what should you check against your existing .cursor/rules/ files?
options: Nothing - rules only matter after implementation is finished
Whether the task exposes a convention that isn't documented yet - if so, add it to a rule file before starting, not after
Whether the rules folder currently has too many files in it
Whether any rules need to be deleted before this particular task
cur-a2-feature-delivery-workflow.why: The pipeline explicitly calls for confirming Rules already cover relevant conventions, and adding any missing one before starting rather than after the fact.

cur-a2-feature-delivery-workflow.q: Why does the pipeline require Agent to run the real build/test/lint commands and paste actual output, rather than accepting a claim?
options: It's a formality with no practical benefit
It closes the gap between 'Agent says it works' and demonstrated proof - a claim is never accepted on its own
It's only necessary for tasks dispatched to the cloud
It replaces the need for a final human read-through of the diff
cur-a2-feature-delivery-workflow.why: The pipeline states plainly: never accept a claim that it works - real pasted output from the actual commands is what's required.

cur-a2-feature-delivery-workflow.q: Even after every automated checkpoint (plan, diff review, verified tests, review triage) looks clean, what final step does the lesson insist on?
options: None - the automated checkpoints are considered sufficient at that point
A final personal read of the complete diff yourself, since you are the author of record
Re-running Agent from scratch on the same task to cross-check the result
Disabling BugBot immediately before the PR is merged
cur-a2-feature-delivery-workflow.why: The lesson insists on a final personal read of the full diff even when every earlier checkpoint looked clean, because you remain the author of record for what ships.
